                                              LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES OVER UNIFORMLY DISCRETE
                                                         METRIC SPACES ARE 3-SCHUR


                                                                MAREK CÚTH AND ONDŘEJ F.K. KALENDA




arXiv:2604.01875v1 [math.FA] 2 Apr 2026
                                                   Abstract. We prove that the Lipschitz-free space over any uniformly discrete
                                                   metric space has the 3-Schur property




                                                                              1. Introduction
                                             The study of Lipschitz-free Banach spaces has become an active area of research
                                          over the past two decades. These spaces arise in a variety of contexts and are known
                                          under several names, including Arens-Eells spaces and transportation cost spaces.
                                          One of their key features is that they provide a canonical way to associate a Banach
                                          space F(M ) to a metric space M , allowing metric properties of M to be translated
                                          into functional-analytic properties of F(M ), and vice versa.
                                             A notable result in this direction is a recent theorem of Aliaga et al. [2], which
                                          states that the Lipschitz-free space F (M ) over a complete metric space M has the
                                          Schur property (i.e., weak and norm convergences of sequences coincide) if and only
                                          if M is purely 1-unrectifiable (that is, M contains no bi-Lipschitz copy of a compact
                                          subset of the real line with positive Lebesgue measure, see [2, Corollary 1.12]). For
                                          further results relating properties of F(M ) to those of the underlying metric space
                                          M , we refer the reader, for instance, to [14, 26].
                                             Lipschitz-free spaces also provide examples of Banach spaces exhibiting previ-
                                          ously unknown phenomena. For instance, in [21, Example 8.3], the second author
                                          constructed a Lipschitz-free space that was the first known Banach space with the
                                          1-strong Schur property but not the 1-Schur property. For additional constructions
                                          of Lipschitz-free spaces with novel properties, see, e.g., [19].
                                             In the present paper, we provide a quantitative strengthening of the aforemen-
                                          tioned result of [2] for certain natural subclasses of purely 1-unrectifiable metric
                                          spaces. To achieve this, we employ a quantitative version of the Schur property
                                          introduced in [22]. This approach is part of the broader program of quantitative
                                          functional analysis, which, roughly speaking, aims to replace qualitative implica-
                                          tions by more precise inequalities between appropriately defined quantities.
                                             Let us recall basic quantities related to the Schur property. Given a bounded
                                          sequence (xn ) in a Banach space, we set
                                                                      ca (xn ) = inf diam{xk ; k ≥ n},
                                                                                  n∈N

                                          i.e., ca (xn ) is the oscillation of sequence (xn ). Note that ca (xn ) = 0 if and only if
                                          (xn ) is Cauchy (hence convergent). Hence ca (xn ) measures how far is the sequence

                                             2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. 46B04; 51F30; 54E50 (Primary); 46B80; 46B20
                                          (Secondary).
                                             Key words and phrases. Lipschitz function; Lipschitz-free space; uniformly discrete space;
                                          quantitative Schur property, 1-strong Schur property.
                                                                                        1
2                            M. CÚTH AND O. KALENDA


from being Cauchy. For a bounded sequence (xn ) we further set
                  δ (xn ) = sup{ca (x∗ (xn )) ; x∗ ∈ X ∗ , ∥x∗ ∥ ≤ 1}.
Then δ (xn ) = 0 if and only if (xn ) is weakly Cauchy, so this quantity measures
how far the sequence is from being weakly Cauchy. Following [22] we say that a
Banach space X is c-Schur for some c ≥ 1 if
              ca (xn ) ≤ cδ (xn ) for each bounded sequence (xn ) ⊂ X.
In [22] it is proved that the classical space ℓ1 is 1-Schur and that there are some
Schur spaces which are not quantitatively Schur. Moreover, in [23] it is proved that
X ∗ is 1-Schur whenever X is isometric to a subspace of c0 (Γ) for a set Γ. This
result was recently used to show (for a complete metric space M ) that F (M ) is 1-
Schur provided M is purely 1-unrectifiable and proper (i.e., closed bounded sets are
compact). This follows by combining [25, Proposition 17] and [2, Theorem 3.2]. We
note that there is also another way to quantify the Schur property, inspired by the
notion of 1-strong Schur property from [16]. For details and a precise relationship
of these two ways of quantification, see Section 2 below.
   Recently, in [21] the second author investigated the quantitative Schur property
in Lipschitz-free spaces over uniformly discrete spaces. Note that a uniformly dis-
crete metric space is obviously purely 1-unrectifiable, so its Lipschitz-free space is
Schur by [2]. However, such a metric space is proper if and only if all bounded
subsets are finite, which is very restrictive. On the other hand, the structure of
uniformly discrete spaces is quite simple, so it is natural to ask whether their
Lipschitz-free spaces are automatically quantitatively Schur. In [21] some coun-
terexamples were given witnessing that the constant 1 is in general unreachable.
More precisely, there is a uniformly discrete metric space M (made from a graph
using the shortest-path metric) which is 3-Schur and not c-Schur for any c < 3. In
the present paper we prove that the constant 3 is optimal. More precisely, the main
result is the following:
Theorem 1.1. Let M be a uniformly discrete metric space. Then F(M ) is 3-Schur.
Moreover, the constant 3 is optimal.
   Let us note that our Theorem 1.1 contributes to the recent line of research fo-
cused on Banach space theoretical properties of Lipschitz-free spaces over uniformly
discrete spaces (hereafter referred to as LFUD spaces). This line of research was
initiated in [24, Proposition 4.4], where N. Kalton observed that every LFUD space
is Schur, it enjoys the Radon-Nikodym property, and the approximation property.
One of the major open problems, originally posed by N. Kalton in [24, p. 185], asks
whether every LFUD space has the bounded approximation property (both posi-
tive and negative answer having interesting consequences, see [17, Problem 18] for
further discussion). It is therefore natural to investigate more deeply the structural
properties of LFUD spaces. Several recent results contribute to this direction; for
instance, [5, Corollary 3.7] shows that every element of an LFUD space is a convex
integral of molecules. Moreover, recent works such as [3] and [18] study Lipschitz-
free spaces over nets in Banach spaces, which form an important subclass of LFUD
spaces.
   Theorem 1.1 will be proved in Section 4 below with help of several lemmata.
The following problem remains open.
          LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES OVER UNIFROMLY DISCRETE ARE 3-SCHUR                             3


Question 1.2. Assume M is a complete purely 1-unrectifiable metric space. Is
F(M ) 3-Schur?
   We recall that F(M ) is even 1-Schur if M is additionally proper. Our main
results provides a positive answer for uniformly discrete spaces. But there are
many complete purely 1-unrectifiable spaces which are neither uniformly discrete
nor proper. In particular, the following special cases remain open.
Question 1.3.       (i) Assume that M is a complete discrete metric space (i.e., a
       complete space without isolated points, not necessarily uniformly discrete).
       Is F(M ) 3-Schur?
  (ii) Let X be an infinite-dimensional Banach space (for example X = ℓ1 , X =
       c0 or X = ℓ2 ). Let p ∈ (0, 1). Define a new metric on X by d(x, y) =
              p
       ∥x − y∥ , x, y ∈ X. Is F(X, d) 3-Schur?
   We complete our main result by a further special case.
Theorem 1.4. Let M be a complete 0-hyperbolic purely 1-unrectifiable metric
space. Then F(M ) is 1-Schur.
   We recall that a metric space (M, d) is 0-hyperbolic if
    ∀x, y, z, u ∈ M : d(x, y) + d(z, u) ≤ max{d(x, z) + d(y, u), d(x, u) + d(y, z)}.
The proof is made by combining two known results and is given below in Section 5.
   A special subclass of 0-hyperbolic spaces is formed by ultrametric spaces. Recall
that a metric space (M, d) is ultrametric if it satisfies the following stronger version
of triangle inequality:
                      ∀x, y, z ∈ M : d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)}.
It is easy to see that any ultrametric space is 0-hyperbolic and it is essentially
known that ultrametric spaces are purely 1-unrectifiable (see Section 5 for more
details), so we have the following corollary.
Corollary 1.5. Let M be an ultrametric space. Then F(M ) is 1-Schur.
   Let us note that one could also investigate quantitative estimates of other prop-
erties of Lipschitz-free spaces. For instance, a quantitative version of weak sequen-
tial compactness (WSC), known as C-WSC for C > 0, has been introduced; see,
e.g., [20, 22] for its definition and basic properties. Since it is known that many
Lipschitz-free spaces enjoy the WSC property (see, for example, [4, Corollary 2.5]),
it would be natural to ask which Lipschitz-free spaces are C-WSC for some C ≥ 12 ,
and to determine the optimal constant whenever possible.1 This question appears
to be of interest even in the case of uniformly discrete metric spaces. Indeed, by
Theorem 1.1 and [22, Proposition 1.1], Lipschitz-free spaces over uniformly discrete
spaces are 3-WSC, but it is not clear whether this constant is optimal. On the other
hand, the optimal constant is known for Lipschitz-free spaces over proper purely
1-unrectifiable spaces: these spaces are L-embedded (see [6, Section 6]) and hence
are 21 -WSC by [20, Theorem 1].
   We close this introduction by recalling the basic definitions and results on Lipschitz-
free spaces used below.
   1Note that Lipschitz-free spaces cannot be C-WSC for C < 1 , as this would imply reflexivity
                                                                2
by [22, Proposition 1.2]. This contradicts the fact that ℓ1 embeds into every infinite-dimensional
Lipschitz-free space, see [10].
4                                  M. CÚTH AND O. KALENDA


Preliminaries on Lipschitz-free spaces: Given a metric space (M, d) with a
distinguished point 0 ∈ M , symbol Lip0 (M ) denotes the spaces of all real-valued
Lipschitz functions on M vanishing at 0 equipped with the norm given by
                                      n |f (x) − f (y)|             o
                ∥f ∥Lip = L(f ) = sup                   ; x ̸= y ∈ M .
                                            d(x, y)
Then Lip0 (M ) is a Banach space. For each x ∈ M , let δ(x) denote the evaluation
functional f 7→ f (x) on Lip0 (M ). The mapping x 7→ δ(x) defines an isometric
embedding of (M, d) into Lip0 (M )∗ . The Lipschitz-free space over M is then defined
by
                    F(M ) := span{δ(x); x ∈ M } ⊂ Lip0 (M )∗ .
Now we recall some basic facts about Lipschitz-free spaces; for their proofs we refer
the interested reader, for instance, to [10, Section 2]. The Lipschitz-free space is
independent of the choice of the distinguished point 0 ∈ M ; that is, Lipschitz-free
spaces constructed with different distinguished points are linearly isometric. Given
0 ∈ N ⊂ M , the natural mapping F(N ) ∋ δ(x) 7→ δ(x) ∈ F(M ), x ∈ N extends to
an isometric embedding, so F (N ) can be identified isometrically with
                                 span{δ(x); x ∈ N } ⊂ F (M ),
and we will use this identification throughout without further mention. If Mf de-
notes the completion of M , then F (M ) and F(M ) are linearly isometric. Hence,
                                                  f
we will often assume without loss of generality that M is complete. The dual space
F(M )∗ is linearly isometric to Lip0 (M ), with the duality given by
                           ⟨f, δ(x)⟩ := f (x),   f ∈ Lip0 (M ), x ∈ M
and extended uniquely from δ(M ) to a continuous linear functional on F (M ) =
span δ(M ). On bounded subsets of Lip0 (M ), the weak∗ topology coincides with
the topology of pointwise convergence. Finally, for C > 0, if M and M ′ are C-
Lipschitz isomorphic metric spaces, then the Banach spaces F (M ) and F (M ′ ) are
C-isomorphic.2

                  2. On quantification of the Schur property
   As recalled in the introduction, a Banach space X is Schur if any weakly con-
vergent sequence is norm convergent. Further, X is called c-Schur (where c ≥ 1) if
ca (xn ) ≤ cδ (xn ) for each bounded sequence (xn ) ∈ X. We will use the following
characterization of the c-Schur property, which easily follows from [21, Proposition
5.1(ic ) ⇐⇒ (iic )].
Lemma 2.1. Let X be a Banach space and let c ≥ 1. Then X is c-Schur if and
only if
             lim sup ∥xn ∥ ≤ c sup{lim sup |x∗ (xn )| ; x∗ ∈ BX ∗ }
                       n                         n
for any bounded sequence (xn ) in X.
   In the literature also another quantification of the Schur property is used. It is so-
called 1-strong Schur property introduced in [16] and used also in [2]. Its c-version
was introduced in [21] and it was compared there with the c-Schur property. So,
we say that a Banach space X has the c-strong Schur property if for any δ ∈ (0, 2]
     2We say f : M → M ′ is C-Lipschitz isomorphism if f is bijection and Lip(f ) · Lip(f −1 ) ≤ C.
If, in addition, M and M ′ are Banach spaces and f is moreover linear, we say f is C-isomorphism.
         LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES OVER UNIFROMLY DISCRETE ARE 3-SCHUR                   5


and any ε > 0 any normalized δ-separated sequence in X admits a subsequence
( 2c
  δ + ε)-equivalent to the standard basis of ℓ1 .
    To formulate its relationship to the c-Schur property, we recall two more quan-
tities. Given a bounded sequence (xn ) in a Banach space, we set
                 ca (xn ) = inf{ca (xnk ) ; (nk ) strictly increasing},
                 e
                   δe (xn ) = inf{δ (xnk ) ; (nk ) strictly increasing}.
  The following proposition follows from [21, Proposition 5.1 and Proposition 5.6].
Proposition 2.2. Let X be a real Banach space and let c ≥ 1.
   (a) The following assertions are equivalent:
         (i) X has the c-strong Schur property;
             ca (xn ) ≤ cδ (xn ) for any bounded sequence (xn ) in X;
        (ii) e
             ca (xn ) ≤ cδe (xn ) for any bounded sequence (xn ) in X.
       (iii) e
   (b) If X is c-Schur, it has also the c-strong Schur property.
   (c) If X has the c-strong Schur property, it is (2c + 1)-Schur.
    We stress that the previous proposition holds only for real Banach spaces. In
the complex case the situation is more complicated and some further changes of
constants are necessary (see [21, Proposition 5.6 and Example 5.9]). Substantial
part of the proof of the previous proposition uses quantitative version of Rosenthal’s
ℓ1 -theorem (see [8] and [21, Section 3]). We restrict ourselves to the real spaces
because Lipschitz-free spaces are over the reals.
    Further, in assertion (c) of the previous proposition the constant 2c + 1 cannot
be replaced by c. This is witnessed by [21, Example 8.3], where a Banach space
of the form F(M ) is exhibited which has the 1-strong Schur property, is 2-Schur
but not c-Schur for c < 2. However, it is not clear, whether the constant 2c + 1 is
optimal or whether it can be replaced by 2c or c + 1.
    The previous proposition also shows that the standard terminology is a bit mis-
leading because the c-strong Schur property is in fact weaker than the c-Schur
property. But we do not attempt to change the terminology.

                               3. Auxilliary results
    In this section we collect some auxilliary results which will be used to prove the
main result. The first lemma enables us to restrict ourselves to bounded spaces. It
is formulated for general metric spaces.
Lemma 3.1. Let (M, d) be a metric space and let c ≥ 1. Then F(M ) is c-Schur
if and only F (A) is c-Schur for each bounded subset A ⊂ M .
Proof. If A ⊂ M , then F (A) is isometric to a subspace of F (M ). Since the c-Schur
property is inherited by subspaces, the ‘only if’ part follows.
   To prove the ‘if part’, assume that F(A) is c-Schur for each bounded A ⊂ M .
Let 0 ∈ M be a distinguished point. For k ∈ Z let Ak = {x ∈ M ; d(x, 0) ≤ 2k }.
Then A Lk is a bounded
                         subset of M , hence F (Ak ) is c-Schur for each k. Thus
Y =       k∈Z F(A  )
                  k ℓ   is c-Schur as well by [21, Theorem 7.4]. Given ε > 0, by
                      1
[24, Proposition 4.3] F(M ) is (1 + ε)-isometric to a subspace of Y . Now we easily
conclude that F(M ) is c-Schur.                                                   □
   The next lemma concerns only uniformly discrete spaces and enables us to re-
strict ourselves to integer-valued metrics.
6                                 M. CÚTH AND O. KALENDA


Lemma 3.2. Let (M, d) be a uniformly discrete metric space. Given ε > 0 there
is a metric space (M ′ , d′ ) such that d′ attains only integer values together with a
bijection F : M → M ′ with L(F )L(F −1 ) < 1 + ε.
Proof. (M, d), being uniformly discrete, is δ-separated for some δ > 0. Let c > 0
be given. Define a new metric d′ on M by d′ (x, y) = ⌈cd(x, y)⌉. It is clear that d′
is a metric on M . Moreover,
                    cd(x, y) ≤ d′ (x, y) ≤ cd(x, y) + 1 ≤ (c + 1δ )d(x, y).
                                           1
Now it is enough take c so large such that cδ < ε.                                               □

                             4. Proof of Theorem 1.1
  In this section we provide a proof of our main result. It will be done in two steps.
The first one is contained in the following lemma.
Lemma 4.1. Let N ∈ N. Assume (M, d) is a pointed metric space such that d
attains only values 0, 1, . . . , N . Assume (Fn )∞
                                                  n=0 is a disjoint sequence of finite
subsets of M . Let (γn )∞
                        n=0 be a bounded sequence in F (M ) such that γn is a linear
combination of δ(x), x ∈ Fn . Assume that lim supn ∥γ0 + γn ∥ > c > 0. Then there
is a 3-Lipschitz function g ∈ Lip0 (M ) such that lim supn ⟨g, γ0 + γn ⟩ > c.
Proof. Up to passing to a subsequence we may assume that limn ∥γ0 + γn ∥ = c′ > c
and that ∥γ0 + γn ∥ < c′ + 1 for each n ∈ N.
   By Lemma 3.3 we may find, for each n ∈ N, a 1-Lipschitz integer-valued function
fn ∈ Lip0 ({0} ∪ F0 ∪ Fn ) such that ⟨fn , γ0 + γn ⟩ = ∥γ0 + γn ∥.
   Since fn is 1-Lipschitz, necessarily ∥fn ∥∞ ≤ N . Since F0 is finite, there are only
finitely many integer-valued 1-Lipschitz functions on F0 . Thus, up to passing to a
subsequence, we may assume that fn |F0 = fm |F0 for any choice m, n ∈ N.
   Note that fn ({0} ∪ F0 ∪ Fn ) contains 0 and has diameter at most N . Hence, it is
contained in a set of the form {an , an + 1, . . . , an + N } for some an ∈ {−N, . . . , 0}.
Up to passing to a subsequence we may assume that the sequence (an ) is constant.
So, the range of each fn is contained in {a, . . . , a + N }. S
                                                                      ∞
   Now we may glue functions fn to one function f : {0} ∪ n=0 Fn → R by setting
f (0) = 0, f = fn on F0 ∪ Fn . By the above it is a well-defined function. We
proceed by analyzing the Lipschitz constant of f . By construction, f is 1-Lipschitz
on {0} ∪ F0 ∪ Fn for each n ∈ N, because it coincides with fn . Moreover, the range
of f is (contained in) {a, . . . , a + N }, so f is N -Lipschitz. If f is not 1-Lipschitz,
the Lipschitz constant is realized on pairs (x, y), where x ∈ Fm , y ∈ Fn for some
1 ≤ m < n. If f is 3-Lipschitz, we simply extend f to a 3-Lipschitz function g.
So, assume f is not 3-Lipschitz. We will show how to pass to a subsequence and
modify f to a 3-Lipschitz function.

   The second step is contained in the following lemma, which enables us to reduce
the situation to the setting of the preceding lemma.
Lemma 4.2. Let N ∈ N. Assume (M, d) is a pointed metric space such that d
attains only values 0, 1, . . . , N . Assume (µn ) is a bounded sequence in F(M ) such
that lim supn ∥µn ∥ > c > 0. Then there is a 3-Lipschitz function g ∈ Lip0 (M ) such
that lim supn ⟨g, µn ⟩ > c.
Proof. Let T : F(M ) → ℓ1 (M \ {0}) be the isomorphism provided by Lemma 3.4.
Note that T (δ(x)) = ex for x ∈ M \ {0}. Using the identification via T , we transfer
from ℓ1 (M \ {0}) to F(M ) the notions of a support, w∗ -convergence and restriction
to a subset of M . We recall that w∗ -topology on bounded subsets of ℓ1 coincides
with the topology of pointwise convergence.
   Let (µn ) and c be as in the statement. Up to passing to a subsequence we may
assume that lim ∥µn ∥ = c′ ∈ (c, ∞). Up to passing to a further subsequence we
10                               M. CÚTH AND O. KALENDA

                         w∗
may assume that µn −→ µ for some µ ∈ F(M ) with ∥µ∥ ≤ c′ . Fix ε > 0 such that
c′ − 9ε > c. Pick a finite F0 ⊂ M \ {0} with ∥µ|M \F0 ∥ < ε. Since µn → µ pointwise
and F0 is finite, up to omitting a finite number of elements from the sequence, we
may assume that ∥(µn − µ)|F0 ∥ < ε for n ∈ N.
   Now, we shall show that passing to a subsequence we may assume there are
pairwise disjoint finite sets Fn ⊂ M \ F0 such that
(2)                           ∥µn |M \(F0 ∪Fn ) ∥ < ε,   n ∈ N.
Indeed, we start by putting n1 := 1 and picking finite F1 ⊂ M \ F0 satisfying
∥µ1 |M \F ∥ < ε whenever F ⊃ F0 ∪ F1 . For the inductive step, assume nj ∈ N and
Fj ⊂ M for j ≤ k were defined. Since ∥µ|M \F0 ∥ < ε and µn → µ pointwise, we
pick nk+1 > nk such that for every n ≥ nk+1 we have ∥µn |Sk Fi ∥ < 2ε . Next,
                                                                 i=1
                                                                   Sk+1
we pick Fk+1 ⊂ M \ (F0 ∪ . . . ∪ Fk ) such that for every F ⊃ i=1 Fi we have
∥µnk+1 |M \F ∥ < 2ε . Then ∥µnk+1 |M \(F0 ∪Fk+1 ) ∥ < ε. This finishes the inductive
construction.
   Denote γ0 := µ|F0 and γn := µn |Fn for n ∈ N, by the above those are points in
F(M ) with finite disjoint supports. Further, we have
      ∥γ0 + γn ∥ ≥ ∥γ0 + µn |M \F0 ∥ − ε > ∥µn |F0 + µn |M \F0 ∥ − 2ε = ∥µn ∥ − 2ε.
Consequently, lim supn ∥γ0 + γn ∥ ≥ c′ − 2ε. By Lemma 4.1 there is a 3-Lipschitz
function g ∈ Lip0 (M ) with lim sup ⟨g, γ0 + γn ⟩ > c′ − 3ε. For every n ∈ N we have
        ⟨g, µn ⟩ = ⟨g, µ|F0 ⟩ + ⟨g, µn |Fn ⟩ + ⟨g, (µn − µ)|F0 ⟩ + g, µn |M \(F0 ∪Fn )
                ≥ ⟨g, γ0 + γn ⟩ − 3 ∥(µn − µ)|F0 ∥ − 3 µn |M \(F0 ∪Fn )
                > ⟨g, γ0 + γn ⟩ − 6ε.
Hence
            lim sup ⟨g, µn ⟩ ≥ lim sup ⟨g, γ0 + γn ⟩ − 6ε > c′ − 9ε > c.
This completes the proof.                                                                □
     Now we are ready to complete the proof of the main theorem.
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Assume that M is a uniformly discrete metric space. We
want to prove that F (M ) is 3-Schur. By Lemma 3.1 we may assume that M is
bounded. By Lemma 3.2 we may additionally assume that the metric on M attains
only integer values. In this case M satisfies the assumptions of Lemma 4.2, which
shows that condition from Lemma 2.1 is satisfied with c = 3. Hence F (M ) is
3-Schur.
   Optimality of constant 3 follows from [21, Example 8.5]                     □

                 5. Proofs of Theorem 1.4 and its corollary
   Theorem 1.4 follows essentially by a combination of known results, it follows
immediately from a formally stronger Theorem 5.1 below.
   Before proceeding to the proofs, let us recall that a metric space is 0-hyperbolic
if and only if it embeds into a an R-tree; see [12, Theorems 3.38]. Rather than
recalling the full definition of an R-tree, which requires additional notions, we note
the following convenient characterization: a metric space (T, d) is an R-tree if and
only if it is 0-hyperbolic and connected, see [12, Theorem 3.40].
   Assume now that (T, d) is an R-tree. Then for any x, y ∈ T there is a unique isom-
etry ϕx,y : [0, d(x, y)] → T with ϕx,y (0) = x and ϕx,y (y) = d(x, y), see [12, Lemma
         LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES OVER UNIFROMLY DISCRETE ARE 3-SCHUR                    11


3.20]. Finally, given A ⊂ T , we say A has length measure zero if λ(ϕ−1
                                                                     x,y (A)) = 0 for
every x, y ∈ T . We refer the interested reader to [12] for more details concerning
R-trees and to [15] for more details concerning the length measure on R-trees and
results related to Lipschitz-free spaces in this context.
Theorem 5.1. Let M be a separable complete metric space. Then the following
conditions are equivalent.
    (a) F(M ) is (1 + ε)-isomorphic to a subspace of ℓ1 for every ε > 0.
    (b) M is 0-hyperbolic and purely 1-unrectifiable.
Consequently, if M is complete 0-hyperbolic and purely 1-unrectifiable (and not
neccessarily separable), then F(M ) is 1-Schur.
Proof. The proof follow from two results proved elsewhere. First, by [7, Theorem
1.2], condition (a) holds if and only if M embeds into an R-tree as a set of length
measure zero. Second, by [2, Theorem C] F(M ) is Schur if and only if M is purely
1-unrectifiable. Knowing those two results, the proof is almost immediate.
    Indeed, if (a) holds then F(M ) is Schur, because it isomorphically embeds into
ℓ1 . Hence, M is purely 1-unrectifiable. Moreover, M is 0-hyperbolic because it
embeds into an R-tree. Hence, (b) holds.
    Conversely, if (b) holds then, since M is 0-hyperbolic, it embeds into an R-tree
and if (T, d) is an R-tree and M ⊂ T is purely 1-unrectifiable, then it has lenght
measure zero as otherwise there would be x, y ∈ T with λ(ϕ−1     x,y (M )) > 0, so there
would exist a compact set K ⊂ ϕ−1     x,y (M ) ⊂ [0, d(x, y)] of positive  measure and
ϕx,y (K) ⊂ M would be an isometric copy of a compact subset of the real line with
positive measure, contradicting that M is purely 1-unrectifiable. Hence, M embeds
into an R-tree as a set of length measure zero, so (a) holds.
    For the “Consequently” part, assume M is complete 0-hyperbolic and purely 1-
unrectifiable. Since 1-Schur property can be obviously tested on separable subspaces
and since for any separable subspace Y ⊂ F(M ) we can find N ⊂ M complete and
separable such that Y ⊂ F(N ), we may without loss of generality assume M is
separable. Then, by the already proven part we obtain that F (M ) is (1 + ε)-
isomorphic to a subspace of ℓ1 for every ε > 0, which implies that F(M ) is 1-
Schur.                                                                                □

   A special case when the above applies is when M is an ultrametric space. We
are convinced it is well-known that ultrametric spaces are purely 1-unrectifiable,
but we were not able to find a reference with a suitable proof. For the convenience
of the reader, we therefore include a proof below. We also refer to Remark 5.3 for
an alternative approach to deriving Lemma 5.2 from existing results; however, this
approach appears somewhat cumbersome.
Lemma 5.2. Any ultrametric space is purely 1-unrectifiable.
Proof. Step 1. Assume that K ⊂ R is a compact set of positive measure. Given
ε > 0, there are real numbers a < b such that λ(K ∩ [a, b]) > (1 − ε)(b − a).
   This is an immediate consequence of Lebesgue density theorem. But in fact, this
statement is elementary, so we provide an easy proof.
   The assertion is obvious if K contains an interval. So, assume it does not contain
an interval, i.e., it is totally disconnected. Set α = min K, β = max K and m =
λ(K). Then α < β, in fact β − α > m. [α, β] \ K is a nonempty open set, so it is a
12                             M. CÚTH AND O. KALENDA


disjoint union of open intervals. This family of intervals must be countable (as we
are in R) and infinite (otherwise K contains an interval). So, say
                                                 ∞
                                                 [
                                [α, β] \ K =             (αn , βn ).
                                                n=1
For n ∈ N define
                                 n

                                 k=1                                   k=1
clearly εn → 0. Further, set

Moreover, An is a finite union of singletons and closed intervals. So, there is one of

                                                m

Since m+ε   n
              ↗ 1, the assertion follows.
   Step 2. Assume that K ⊂ R is a compact set of positive measure. Let d be
a metric on K such that (K, d) is ultrametric and d(x, y) ≤ |x − y| for x, y ∈ K.
Given ε > 0 there are x, y ∈ K such that d(x, y) < ε |x − y|.
   Fix n ∈ N, n ≥ 3. By Step 1 there are real numbers a < b such that λ(K∩[a, b]) >
(1 − n1 )(b − a). Let a = t0 < t1 < · · · < tn = b be the equidistant partition. By
the choice of a, b for each j ∈ {1, . . . , n} there is some xj ∈ K ∩ (tj−1 , tj ). Then
d(xj , xj+1 ) ≤ |xj+1 − xj | < n2 (b − a) for j = 1, . . . , n − 1. The ultrametric property
yields d(x1 , xn ) < n2 (b − a). On the other hand, |x1 − xn | > (1 − n2 )(b − a). Thus,
                                            2
                              d(x1 , xn )          2
                                          < n 2 =     .
                              |x1 − xn |   1− n   n−2
        2
Since n−2  → 0, the assertion follows.
   Step 3. Completion of the proof.
   Assume (M, d) is ultrametric which is not purely 1-unrectifiable. Then there is
a compact K ⊂ R of positive measure and a bi-Lipschitz embedding f : K → M .
For x, y ∈ K define ρ(x, y) = d(f (x), f (y)). Then (K, ρ) is ultrametric and ρ is
Lipschitz-equivalent to the euclidean metric. This contradicts Step 2.
                                                                                □
Remark 5.3. An alternative approach to deriving Lemma 5.2 from existing results
is the following. Pick an ultrametric space M . Since completion of an ultrametric
space is ultrametric, we may without loss of generality assume M is complete.
Moreover, obviously M is purely 1-unrectifiable if and only if each of its compact
subsets is, so we may assume M is compact. At this point, there are at least two
ways to conclude. First, by [9, Theorem 2] the space F(M ) is isomorphic to ℓ1 , so
it is Schur and M is purely 1-unrectifiable by [2, Theorem D]. Alternatively, one
          LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES OVER UNIFROMLY DISCRETE ARE 3-SCHUR                            13


may apply [11, Theorem 3.7] which asserts that F (M ) is isometric to a dual space,
and then invoke [2, Theorem B].
Proof of Corollary 1.5. Let M be ultrametric. Its completion is easily seen to be
ultrametric as well, so without loss of generality M is complete. It is clear that
M is 0-hyperbolic. Further, by Lemma 5.2 M is purely 1-unrectifiable, so we may
conclude by Theorem 1.4.                                                        □
